New York, April 16-The brewery


lockout has begun, and more than


5000 brewers, brewery wagon drivers,


masters, helpers, wagon-makers,
coopers. painters and apprentices in
this city, Brooklyn, Jersey City,
Newark, Paterson and Staten Islam d
are out of work.


The financial week of the working
men ended at noon to-day. According


to the instructions of the unions every


brewer in every one of the above


named cities returned to work as


usual this morning, and there were
few outward indications that
THE GREATEST LOCKOUT
That has ever occurred in this sec.
tion of the country would occur ina
few hours.


Just after noon the proprietors of
each brewery met the men and in
formed them that their services were
no longer wanted, that they had


unanimously decided to be their own
bosses and would not submit to any
thing dictatorial from their men.
However, if the men sought re-em-
ployment as individuals and would
disconnect themselves from the unions


they would get work. The men passed
quietly TO the cashiers desks after
they had heard what the proprietor


had to say, received their weekly pay


and departed at noon. According to


the agreement every brewery door


closed and business for the time is


suspended.

able intrenchments which are manned

masese is now at Mulinun under the pro-

The steamboat John II. Hanna. from Qua
chita river, with large number of passengers
and cargo of 500 bales of cotton on board, was
burned Monday night at Plaquemine, Miss,
liz miles above New Orleans Many Of the
crew and passengers were asleep when the fire
broke out and spread with indescribable rapid
ity. John Cullen, a stoker, seeing flames
bursting from the tiers of cotton near the
boiler, ran to the engine-room and gave the
alarm Clerk Powell ran through the smoke,
which filed the cabin, and kicked at the doors,
and in a short time almost everybody was awake.
Then confusion worse COMPOUNDED appeared,
and frantic people on the boat ran to different
exits to make their escape. but the boat was
filled high with cotton and the passageways
were filed with smoke. Many dropped before
they were able to get to the forward part of the
boat and were dead when the steamer went
down


Then, to add to the CONSERVATION steam
pipe burst and filled the boat with scalding
steam. Engineer Merriman was forced to
abandon his post. As soon as the flames began
to shoot up the sides of the boat. Capt Jolles,
the pilot headed the boat for the shore. and
the boat was soon run into the bank. When
the Hanna struck she bounded away again and
swung around, drifting down as she burned


Floating cotton, charred timber and other
debris filed the river, and many people were
struggling desperately in the water for their
lives. Some of them we're able to swim ashore,
but most OF them were so badly burned or so
thoroughly exhausted that they struggled but
few minutes and sank to rise no more. As the
burning boat struck the bank of the river the
crew and passengers who had been able to
reach the forward end of the boat sprang
ashore. some of them with scorched faces and
bruised limbs and many of them with scarcely
any covering.


Among those who managed to get off were
Capt. Holmes and Bob Smith. the unfortunate
pilot of the Inflated White, who was passen-
ger. When the captain jumped ashore he was
horribly burned, and buried his face and hands
In the soft mud and begged piteously for some
one to help him. Smith Just behind. and
was laid out by the side of the dying captain.
Nothing could be done for the suffering men,
and the two died together on the river bank.


The struggling unfortunates who reached
shore were taken care of, and doctors and
Others came to their assistance and tried to
alleviate their sufferings.


No one saw Clerk Powell, who displayed
much heroism in waking up the passengers,
after he had raped at the doors, and it is
quite positive that he was burned to death and
went down with the steamer. The boat burned
rapidly after she reached the bank, and in a
very short time she sank.


Among those that were lost are: Captain
Holmes, master of the boat; Samuel Powell
chief clerk; Bob Smith, a pilot from Smith
land, La: Mike O'Neil, night Waterman; Joe
Crane, cabin Waterman; Monroe Deck, first
COOK; JACK DuH, second COOK; Joe harvey,
cabin boy; Jim Watson, second baker; John
Grafton, carpenter.


Among those who were badly burned are:
Dan Carroll. steward; Jim O'Neill. deck hand;
John Gibbons, sailor-man; Louis WEIGH. roust-
about, and number of others.


Coming down on the boat as passengers were
a number of the crew of the steamer Josie W.,
all of whom were saved. The survivors were
all warm in their praise of the humane people
of Plaquemine. who spared no pains and no
money to furnish them with clothes and shelter
after their terrible experience.


None of the men could say what was the
origin of the fire. The general impression,
however. is that some careless smoker threw a
cigarette among the cotton bales and thereby
caused the disaster


1t is believed that the total loss of life was
about thirty

mally, is drier and more bracing than that Of

rings, scarf pins, jeweled bracelets, presenta-
ton swords, photographs of himself framed

lains, secretaries, station masters, traffic enRi-

people who could not be decorated, or who,
having been rewarded already with decorations

to insignia of higher class

official entitled him to keepsake, while the
servants of the various foreign sovereiens
whom the emperor visited were, of course, re-
warded with money. Thus the coachmen who
habitually drove the emperor about Stuttgart,
Munich and Vienna received 1000 marks, or
S25O each. The cooks in all the imperial or
royal households received gold watches and
chains. These were all made of q pattern
double cased, gold, keyless hunters, with
engine-turned backs, and in the center the
imperial crown and cipher. The chains were
of close-twisted links, with bars fashioned like
little pieces Of rope coil The cost Of the
watches and chains was 600 marks, or ESQ

New York, June 29.-At O'Clock this
afternoon there was crush Of beauty at
the Mayors Chambers at the City Hall.
1t was bridal party in which Mrs. Lilly
Warren Hammersley, one Of Americas
handsomest and most wealthy ladies,
and Geo. Chase Spencer Churchill, Duke
Of Marlborough, were the contracting
parties. The party came to the historic
building in carriage, the little Duke
and fascinating widow retiring imme-
diately to one Of the side rooms Of the
Mayors office. Mr.. Ward McAlister and
Mr.. Arthur Leary who were Of the party,
notified the Mayor that he had been
selected to perform the wedding cere-
mony. The Mayor smilingly accepted
the task and bade the wedding party
welcome.


The company consisted Of Ward Nc
Allster and Miss McAllister, Mr.. Fred.
Spedden and Miss Spedden, Mrs. Nichols
Fisk, Arthur Leary, Lawrence Jerome,
Miss Beckwith, Mrs. Kruger, aud Henry
Clews. While the party were gossipping
In the Executive chamber, Speaker John
q. Carlisle and Congressman Timothy J.
Campbell happened In, and were invited
by the Mayor to remain and witness the
ceremony.


At half-past one the necessary certif-
cate having been prepared the bride and
groom entered arm-in-arm in advance OF
Mayor Hewitt to His Honor's roll top
desk in the center OF the room. Mrs.
Hammersley was attired in loose fitting
tailor-made chocolate brown travelling
dress Of tricot cloth, with jaunty turban
to match, at her bosom she wore q spray
of lilies OF the valley. She looked pale
and restless. The Duke wore plain
BLACK cutaway coat with low cut waist
coat, with small white rose in his but
ton-hole. Mr.. Creighton Webb acted as
best man. There were no bridesmaids.


AS the Mayor began reading the mar
riage ceremony, Mrs. Hammersley drew
the long, undressed, light.brown kid
glove from her right hand, and placed
her gloved left in the Dukes palm. Mrs.
Hammersley answered the usual ques-
tions in an indistinct voice, though the
Dukes responses were clear and heard
all around the room.


The ceremony over, the Duke slipped
the wedding-ring on the third finger Of
her ungloved hand. The certificate was
handed to the Duke, and the Mayor said
that with the Dukes permission he
would take his compensation. He took
the newly-made Duchess by the hand,
and she stopped while he planted kiss
upon her lips. The Duchess received
congratulations from her friends, and
after chatting with the wedding party for
few minutes, drove with the Duke up
town. 1t is understood that they will
sail for Europe tomorrow.

NEENAH, Wrs., August 23.-At mid
night last night, large paper mill,
owned by Geo. Whitney on the island
between this city and Menasha was
burned. While the burning structure was
surrounded by a crowd, battery OF
boilers exploded, the roof and walls
were thrown outward, sending shower
of bricks and timber among the
spectators. Eighteen persons were
killed, seven fatally injured and num-
Der less seriously hurt several of
whom will die. The mill, three-story
structure, cost 500, 1000 and was operated
day and night.


When the flames broke out fifty men
were at work in the building. The fire
alarm brought several hundred people to
the spot, who crowded as close to the
burning building as the intense heat
would permit. At about 80 A. NJ,
while the building was mass of flame,
the explosion occurred. Without warn
ing the roof was thrown upward, and the
outward walls of the brick crumbled and
crashed into the street in an instant.
Scores of men were buried under the de-
bris. There was moment of silence,
then


A CRY OF HORROR


From the multitude. The first strong
impulse to fly from possible further dan
ger was soon overcome, and hundreds
began the work of recovering the bodies
of the dead and rescuing the injured.
Body after body was found crushed and
mangled by the great timbers and
masonry almost beyond recognition.
The injured were carried to neighboring
residences and their homes as soon as
their identity could be fixed.


HOW THE ACCIDENT OCCURRED.


The fire started from the shavings in
the engine room. After the roof fell the
iremen turned the hose upon an i'm
.mense revolving iron bleacher filled with
straw rags superheated. An explosion
followed. The bleacher was carried two
hundred feet across the tramway where
most of the people were standing, now
ing them down like grass. It passed
about as high as a mans head and most
of those killed and injured were struck
by it on the head

Joseph Bridges, VIM. Gueltz, Thomas
Dourgais, Frank Shelter, Gilbert Mericle,
Chris Laighousre, John L Eichowger,

Joe Smith, John Suller, Tingle Soeltz.


Seven OF the killed were coopers by
trade. Nearly all leave large families in
poor circumstances. They will be buried
at the city's expense, probably all to-
gether, next Sunday. The mayor ap-
pealed to the citizens for aid for the des-
titute families. A coroner's Jury has
been impaneled and will investigate.

PRECIOUS STONES.


From the jewelers. Weekly.


Many people believe that diamond can be
heated white hot in good fire with impunity,
but wouldn't advise them to try the expert
ment too often. l have seen diamonds which
had passed through the great fire at Chicago
They were covered with white film and looked
like pieces of alum. After passing through the
polisher's hands they were apparently as good
as new, but still fancied that there was a GER
tain loss of luster and feel sure that second
heating would have made this still more plainly
perceptible. How high a heat will rubies and
sapphires stand? Well I've carefully heated
some dark-colored sapphires and been rewarded
by seeing them cool off several shades lighter
Upon the color of others heat made not the
least impression.


was obliged To be very careful in heating
and in letting the stones cool, as any sudden
variation in temperature will split them in a
moment. Topaz have destroyed entirely by
heat, and rubies are also easily ruined by high
temperature. Heated white hot and plunged
into water any of the latter stones will split
into thousand fragments; so be careful if you
make any experiments. Pearls should not be
heated either, as the result will resemble oyster
shells more than anything else.

Kamschatkan dogs are probably the most
sagacious of all feral types, and are employed
and trainedin the most careful manner for the
multitudinous services required of them.
Soon after birth they are placed with their
dam in deep pit, that they may see neither
man nor beast, and after having been weaned
are condemned to solitary confinement for six
months, at the end of which time they are put
to a sledge with other dogs, and being ex-
tremely shy and frightened withal, they run
as fast as they can until they become blown
and cowed. After this trial trip they are re-
manded to their pit where they remain, off and
on, until they are thoroughly tired and sledge-
broken. The severe education sours their
temper amazingly and makes them anything
but companionable. Drivers are frequently
obliged to stun them by blow on the nose be-
fore embarrassing them on account of their
savage nature. Besides drawing sledges they
tow boats up rivers in summer and keep their
masters warm in winter nights. They are re-
markable weather prophets, and discount the
Signal Service Bureau, for if, when resting on
journey they dig holes in the snow, there is
certain to be a storm. They are Of husky type,
shaggy, with erect curling bushy tails and not
very sharp noses and ears. They live exclusively
on fish, which they catch for themselves. In
winter their ration comprises forty frozen her
rings per day.

Associated Press Dispatches to the HERALD


ST. LOUIS, November 2S.-A panic oc-
Cured at the Blair Sunday school to-day,
and nothing but the great presence of
mind of the corps of teachers prevented
great loss of life. The steam-heating
apparatus got out of order, and the rat
tling in the coils, coupled with escaping
steam, alarmed the children, who, fear
ing an explosion, started for the door.
Miss Bettina Krebs, the teacher in
charge, got to the door first and pre-
| vented stampede. Scarcely had order
been restored, however, when the noise
in the steam pipes was repeated with in
creased violence, and before Miss Bet
tina Krebs could reach the door second
time, the terror-stricken children had
gained the hall. The faithful teacher
was borne to the floor and trampled
upon, sustaining serious injuries. The
excitement spread to room No. 10, lust
opposite, presided over by Miss Clara
Sickle, and the children became un-
manageable there. The shutting of feet
and the kissing Of escaping steam spread
the panic to room No. IA, Miss Mary P.
Miller teacher, and she, too, was
thrown from her feet and tram
pied upon. The janitor appeared on
the scene and did rough but heroic
work in preventing the children from
trampling each other to death. A pupil
in room No. Is raised the cry of fire, and
the pupils made rush for the hall.
Miss Cullen, the teacher, with commend
able presence of mind and heroic efforts,
quelled the disturbance, and in short
time order was restored. Two of the
teachers. Miss Miller and Miss Krebs,
were badly injured by being trampled
upon. Seven pupils were injured.
Birdie Weakened was so badly trampled
upon that she had to be removed in an
ambulance Annie Dodge received severe
internal injuries and external bruises;
Annie Meyers had her head badly gashed
on the stone steps Emma Delendorf, left
arm broken Ruth Reilly, serious internal
injuries; Ida Klostermeyer, Australia
Stoche and Elsie Mcbride, badly bruised,
but not seriously injured. The panic
created intense excitement, and many
parents hurried to the school building to
look after their children.

missiOners, Kern and Reynolds, are Democrats and

reason influence was brought to bear from all
sides, but without effect the Grand Jurors
resisting all cajolery, threats and promises alike

SACRAMENTO, May 1S.-A gasoline ex-
plosion occurred this morning in the
basement of a little brick house sit
uated in the alley between Eighth and
Ninth streets. The upper portion was
occupied by j. B. Greentree, wife and
child, they renting the place from F. F.
Dolan. Dolan had two gasoline stoves in
the basement, and this morning he
lighted one and then went down town.
When he returned the fire had gone out,
but the gasoline had not been turned off
and the room was full of the fumes of
the liquid. Dolan seems to have ignored
this fact, and when he struck match
and attempted to light the second stove
there was a terrific explosion.


The floor gave way beneath Dolan,
and when he scrambled from beneath
the debris his hair and whiskers were
partially burned off, one side of his face
was blistered, and one of his hands
almost cooked. A large hole was blown
through the floor above and plastering
knocked in large patches from the walls
and ceiling.


Mrs. Greentree and child were in the
kitchen above where the stove had been
located, but escaped with slight injuries.

while the hours along.

dove;

love.

ows hover nigh;

SAN Francisco, September 2.-An Er.
ominer special from West Superior, Wis.
says: Early this morning fire was dis.
covered in the American House. Water
was not turned on the fire until the en-.
tire building was enveloped in mass Of
flames. The screams of the frantic men
and women escaping from the burning
building, some in only their night clothes
lent horror to the scene. The fire was
finally gotten under control and confined
to the hotel. At least six persons
were burned to death; perhaps
more. Three bodies were taken out this
afternoon. Only one was identified.
Half a dozen men appeared at the Sec
ond story windows, and three of them


jumped to blankets spread for them in
the street, the others falling back into
the flames. One man carried the pros
trate form of his bed fellow whom he
was unable to arouse, out of the burning
hotel and laid him down. The fellow
suddenly realized the situation and with
a wild yell rushed back into the fire,
Several men who were asleep in the
second story are still unaccounted for,
and it is pretty certain they perished.

dentally punctured gas main. They
Lit candle to see what was the mat

slant the seventy odd clerks and GUS

front and piles of ready

Electric railways may be very good things.
but until the engineers learn how to control
the electricity, they will be regarded with
suspicion.


The other day a lady who was riding on
the electric line between BROOKLYN and
Jamaica took a seat near the box through
which the electricity passed. The car had
Travelled but short distance when the ladv
heard two reports like those of pistol. and
almost instantly bright blue flame shot in
through the window. She made dive for
her two children, when the skin was suds
denly scorched OFF the first finger of her left
hand, and the hand itself felt as though n
had been cut with knife. All the electric
lights went out and the passengers rushed
from the car. They were persuaded to re-
turn, but just as they took their
seats there was another report, and the
lady's left knee was drawn up to her chest
so that she could neither move nor straiebten
herself. She was carried home, and her
physicians declared that she was disabled for
life. When the matter was reported to the
officials of the company they made light of
it, notwithstanding the fact that one of
the engineers had his leg torn open by
shock few days before.


If the facts in this case have been cor
rectly reported, the public will cone to the
conclusion that there is considerable danger
in electric railway travel. Electricity is a.
trichsy spirit, and no man has yet found out
how to control it.

place. Early in the day a steady

nightfall. The sidewalks and streets
were consequently deluged with mud,

able day If the season. In view of this

Donovan set the ball rolling by landing

Dempsey returned on the stomach

scientific. Every one was electrified by

men separated without attempting
any fighting. Dempsey sent stingccr

another clinch followed. Dempsey
rushed at Donovan, who landed on his
lace, but got one in the stomach for his
pains. Donovan found Dempsey's neck
with his left just as time was called.


Sixth and last round-Both men came
up slightly distressed, showing plainly
the effects of the work. Donovan found
Dempsy's stomach with his left when a
clinch ensued. After the break Dono-
van landed on Dempsey's neck
with his right, and then sent
his left out straight on Dempsey's nose.

A ssociated Press DISPATCHES to the HERALD
SUAKlx, December 20.-The combined
force of the British and Egyptians made
an attack yesterday upon the rebel posi-
ton. They stormed the redoubts and
trenches, and after brilliant engage
ment lasting half an hour, drove the en-
emy into the brush. The rebels reported
their loss thousand killed. The British
encamped in the rebel position. The
victory is complete. The British
lost four killed and two wound
cd. During the gallant cavalry
charge the Egyptian and Black regi-
ments charged the trenches and carried
them brilliantly, loeing two killed, thirty
wounded. The only officers wounded in
the attack were two Egyptians. The
rebel loss is now stated to be four
hundred.


Before dawn the British man-of. war
Startling and an Egyptian steamer
moved up the coast, with orders to cover
the rebels at Handoub. At daybreak the
forts opened fire upon the rebel trenches,
and the troops advanced to the attack,
the Black Brigade on the right flank, the
cavalry and mounted infantry covering
them. The Scottish Borderers and the
Welch Regiment and the Egyptian Brig
ade occupied the embankment between
the forts. The British infantry was held
in reserve. The forts shelled the
trenches, keeping up terrific
firing. The enemy held his ground with
intense courage until the Black Brigade
charged the trenches, which fell after
half-hour's hard fighting. The rebels
fought with fanatical bravery. Two of
the enemy's guns were captured. The
Naval Brigade did splendid work. The
Scottish Borderers are now at work
entrenching the rebel position, the
enemy retreating toward Hasheen and
lamar. The British force numbers
1900.


The hussars, who followed the flying
Arabs. returned after chasing the enemy
to within four miles of Handoub. The
enemy is still flying.


THE STANDARDS STORY.


The Standards Suakim special says
At 430 this morning the man-of-war
Racer opened battle by shelling the ene-
my's trenches. The ships up the coast
followed suit and landed parties, who
lighted fires and placed dummies in po-
sition. This had the effect of deceiving
the enemy coming from Handoub. The
whole force moved towards the enemy's
left flank with the naval detachment
with machine guns; the cavalry and
mounted infantry scouting and protect
ing the TANKS and rear. The two lines
comprising the battallions in double COM
panies rushed towards the left corner of
the enemy's trench; the British infantry
and Egyptian reserve lining the embank-
ment between the water forts. General
Grenfell and staff occupied the position
to the left of the water forts. From 5
O'Clock a heavy salvo of guns and NOR
tars from every fort bore on the trenches.


THE SITUATION AT THE CLOSE.


The trenches are nearly filled and two
temporary redoubts are being built for
the joint forces. They will bivouac on
the field to night.


The naval detachment with the
machine guns, remain in the trenches.
The man. .of-war Startling has been sent
and all the available steamers to anchor
off Handoub, in order to prevent the
force from Handoub coming upon the
troops. During the action the Dervishes
were severely punished. A quiet night
is expected.


Osman Digna's nephew and twelve
Dervishes have been captured, and all
are wounded. Serious complaints are
made concerning the quality of the
sabres and revolvers furnished to the
troops. Several cavalrymen returned
with broken sabres and in many in
stances their revolvers became clogged
and rendered useless.


THE TORY DILEMMA.


LONDON, December 20.-In speech
at Scarborough, Lord Salisbury said the
Ministry had no intention of entangling
the country in Soudan expedition, but
they could not abandon Suakim. As long
as the Kbedive desires, England will
maintain the Red Sea ports. It would be
madness to surrender Suakim when they
were on the verge of suppressing slavery.
By the Treaty of Paris, England is bound
to uphold the integrity of the Sultan's
empire.


LATEST OF THE FIGHT.


LONDON, December 20.-A dispatch
from Suakim says: A feature of the
fighting was the determined rush upon
the trenches by the Blacks and
Egyptians. The Dervishes fought with
the utmost bravery, great many
Of them dying in the trenches. The
charge of the Hussars is also specially
mentioned. When the Dervish cavalry
saw them coming they dismounted and
planted their spears in the ground, but
this proved no obstruction to the Hussars,
who swept down upon the Dervish horse
men like an avalanche, cut through their
ground. The Hussars then reformed
and charged the remaining Dervishes,
who fed. A large portion Of the rebel
forces were not engaged in to-day's fight
ing, being absent, camping at Handoub
and the Wells beyond. 1t is believed
the rebels will be enforced and make an
attempt to retake their last position.

The trial of Henry Stevens and Christian
kindtner for arson in the Mexican County.

domestic ties on record. Henry Stevens in
1866 was the mate Of an Atlantic steamer. On

he fell in love with young German girl. a
steerage passenger, whose name was Pauline
Baumann. The girl reciprocated the officers
affection, and on landing in New York they
were married. The bride was on her way 70

known lumber village. Stevens quit the service
OF the steamship company and Joined his for
tunes with those of his bride.


Not long afterward the Bradford region be-
gan TO attract the attention of oil operators
and Stevens and his wife opened boarding
house. They were still keeping boarders in
1873, when dashing German named Christian
kindtner became an inmate of the house He
fell in love with his landlady. She was induced
by him to believe that she was not happy with
her husband, and she obtained divorce from
Stevens. The latter seems to have regarded
this proceeding with remarkable complacence,
Tor he did not leave the house. Mrs. Stevens
married kindtner but on the wedding night
for some reason deserted him and returned to
the guardianship of her first husband In a
short time she procured divorce from Kindt-
ner and remarked Stevens. Kindtner did not
let the sudden ending of his honeymoon and
the utter reputation and legal separation OF
his bride worry him apparently, Tor he con-
tinued to board with the Steyenses


Last winter Henry Reagan, a well-to-do land
scape gardener, of Bradford, advertised for a
wife. His advertisement was read by Mrs.
Hannah Young, a comedy middle-aged widow Of
Indianapolis. She replied to it, and the result
was that she came to Bradford and married
Gardener keggan. The Widow Young had
seventeen-year-old son named Robert. He was
a good-looking boy, large for his age. The
neighbors. Mrs. Stevens, although nearly fifty
years OF age, fell in love with the boy Robert
Young. Her charms at the same time infatu-
ated Robert. Again Mrs. Stevens had resort 10
the divorce court, and, as the divorce laws Of
Pennsylvania accommodate themselves to cir
cumstances, she was speedily released from the
bonds that had made her for the second
time Henry Stevens wife. She then
married Robert Young and established
her youthful spouse as the head of
her boarding house. Stevens accepted the
situation with commendable stoicism, and took
his place with Kindtner, the other dethroned
husband, as boarder in the house. Things
ran on smoothly until last summer, when Mrs.
Young took her boy-husband and her effects
and with his mother and stepfather removed
to another part OF the city. where the combi-
nation opened public house known as Dargle
Park. This left ex-Husbands Stevens and
kindtner out in the cold, and they protested
loudly, but without avail. few weeks ago
the Dargle Park House, together with all the
buildings connected with il, was destroyed by
fire. The fire was plainly of incendiary origin,
and Mrs. Young, charging her late husbands,
Stevens and kindtner, with having fired the
building, had them arrested They were in
dicted and their trial came off at the last term
OF court The evidence against them was in
sufficient to convict them, but during the trial
this curious domestic history was made public

SAN Francisco, August 24.-The fight
between Peter jackson, the colored
champion heavy weight of Australia, and
George Godfrey, the col ored pugilist of
Boston, which occurred here this even
ing, had been looked forward to with the
greatest interest in sporting circles for
more than a month, and as conse-
quence, the rooms of the California Ath-
letic Club was crowded when the men
stepped into the ring. The contest was
under Marquis of Queensbury rules for
purse of $4,000. Hiram Cook, of this
city, acted as referee. A great difference
in the size Of the two men was very
noticeable when they faced each other
in the ring. Jackson appeared to be three
or four inches taller than his opponent
and weighed thirty pounds more. In ad-
dition to this his long reach. gave him an
advantage which Godfrey could not
overcome, and with few exceptions the
fell short. Both men opened
was maintained till the close.
The only knock down occurred in the
second round, when Jackson upper-cut
his opponent and sent him to the floor.
In the first ten rounds Jackson had
gained decided advantage, though God
frey made him work very hard. In the
last three rounds the punishment which
Godfrey received was terrible. Jackson
rushed him around the ring and forced
him against the ropes, all the time
raining fearful blows upon his head and
trying in vain to beat him to the floor.
Blood was flowing very freely from God
frey's face, and in the nineteenth round
he saw there was no possibility of his re-
turning any of the punishment, and he
gave up the fight.

ST. PETERSBURG, October 31.-The Off
cial statement regarding the accident to
the Cars train Monday is as follows
The train containing the Gar and
Czarina and suite left Taranorka at noon
Monday. While passing through deep
gorge near Borki the train left the rails.
At the time of the accident the Gear and
Czarina were in the saloon carriage at
breakfast. When the first carriage left
the track the rest of the train oscillated
and the succeeding carriage keeled over.
The saloon carriage, although remaining
on the track, was badly shattered. The
roof fell in, but restedon portion of the
side, thus forming shield for the occu-
pants.


1t seems Incredible, with such havoc,
that any occupants OF the train should
have escaped. But God protected the
Gar and his family, who were taken
from the debris uninjured. Some of the
other occupants of the train received
slight contusions. The only person Sc
verely injured was General Schereme-
heff, Aide. de- Camp Of the Czar.


The Grashdanin states the train was
drawn by two engines, and consisted of
several carriages besides the saloon car
riage, the latter OF massive construction.
The train was running at sixty-five versts
an hour.


When the first engine left the track it
plowed up the roadbed and embedded it.
self in the earth. The second engine
ran on top of the first and was wrecked.

wrecked. They were occupied by court
servants and railway officials, among
whom were Baron st. Joinval, Chief In
spector of Railroads, who was badly in
jured. Generals Vannoxski and Tchere-

scene some time giving attention to the
injured. Towards evening they returned
to Zosowoje, the last station they left.
Religious services have been held
throughout the Empire, giving thanks
for the escape of the Imperial family.
The Grashdanin contradicts the official
report of the accident in regard to the
casualties. 1t afirms that twenty per.

HOW SOME FAMILIES GET THEIR COAL WITHOUT

In South Washington, where the coal-cars
are unloaded, many tons of coal are lost to the
dealers during the year. In the section known
as BLOOD Field" can be seen almost any morn
ing two or three dozen boys and girls, with
baskets and bags, looking for free fuel. They
pick up from along the tracks the coal which
is dropped from the cars while being unloaded
and then follow the carts through the streets
to bag any Jumps that may drop when the
vehicles strikes a stone or a rough place in the
street. Then when the driver is not looking
they will grab coal from the CARTS In this way
many children succeed in gathering enough
fuel to run the fires at home during the entire
year. When a crowd strikes a driver who is
asleep ON his cart they have a ''snap," and it
takes but few minutes to fill their bag or
basket. Sometimes the police interfere and ar
rest them, but most of them conduct their steal
ing the year round without detection. The same
thing Is practiced to some extent on the Balti-
more and Ohio railroad Sometimes the cars
run short, because the coal is stolen before
they are unloaded- Every now and then COM
plants are made, and railroad detectives are
sent here to protect the freight. Then num-
Der OF arrests are made, and for several days
the coal gatherers make themselves scarce
But when the detectives leave they usually
know 1t, and operations are renewed.

Associated Press DISPATCHES to the HERALD


BIRMINGHAM, Ala, November 1.-two
funerals took place here yesterday which
were largely attended and formed a eli
max Of an extraordinary tragedy. Rob-
ert Nabors was prominent physician at
Montevallo, in this State, and w. w.
Shortridge was successful lawyer in the
same place. Both were young men.
Some time ago Nabors employed Short
ridge to collect few claims against de-
linquent patients. The returns were not
satisfactory and the men quarreled, but
parted without coming to blows.


Last Saturday Nabors called at Short
ridges Office and the old trouble broke
out afresh. They finally agreed to fight
with bowie knives in darkened room
just off the Office. Removing their coats
and shoes the men entered the room and
fought blindly but desperately for nearly
ten minutes. The duel was one of the
most vicious ever reported in Alabama.
The men plunged their knives into each
other until they looked as though they
had been slaughtering beeves. Every
thing in the room was despatched with
blood.


Some persons living in the lower story
heard the noise of the duellists as they
rolled upon the floor, and ran upstairs to
separate the combatants. When the
door was broken open Nabors staggered
into the Office with the blood streaming
rom q dozen gashes in his face and
breast. Without saying word he rushed
down stairs still clasping the CORY knife
in his hand. Lying upon the floor of the
room was Shortridge. His head had
been .slashed in the most dreadful man.
ner. The arteries of his neck had been
severed, one eve had been gouged out,
and his hands were cut so terribly that
the fingers hung only by the tendons.
The man was dead.


Majors, after leaving the Office ran out
on the street, where his bleeding face
snd CORY garments spread CONSERVATION
among the Negroes. He seemed to be
cTazed with pain and staggered wildly
along the street until he reached store
where Albert Keenan,, Negro, stood in
tne doorway. Without saying word,
MAJORS rushed at Keenan, and struck
him with the knife The Negro ran into
the store where the now thoroughly
insane man made another desperate
lunge at him. Keenan, seized q gun
which was lying upon the counter
and then turned to face the madman,
who was in the act of making another
lunge with his knife. The two men
clinched, but Nabors, who was weak
from loss of blood, was no match for his
ANTAGONIST and was quickly thrown upon
the floor.


Before Nabors could get upon his feet
again Keenan, dealt him terrible blow
upon the head with the stock of his gun
and then leaping over his body ran into
the street and out of town. Nabors never
negained consciousness. His skull had
been fractured. He died at midnight
Keenan, cannot be found.

NoGALEs, September 20.-Further par
ticulars Of the disaster at the San Geroni-
mo mine, Sonora, on Monday last, state
that Superintendent Melle was killed
outright. His death did not result from
a cavern of the mine, as at first sup
posed, but by a cave-in of the ground
beneath his office. Melle had just gone
into the office to arrange for paying off
the employees. The men were standing
about outside the office when the ground
suddenly gave way and precipitated the
Office and Superintendent into the old
workings, several hundred feet below the
surface. The employees all managed to
escape. After considerable labor the re-
mains OF Melle were exhumed.

WASHINGTON, October 1.-THE Ameri-
can Street Railway Association met to-
day. The delegates present represented
nearly every city of prominence. Presi-
dent Holmes, of Chicago, delivered the
annual address. The subject of carrying
mails by street cars was considered by
committee. Several roads running be-
tween postoffices have secured the desig-
nation of United States mail carriers
from the Government. The only objec.
tion is the obstructions that occur from
wagons and other traffic. The commit
tee has consulted with the postoffice
authorities, and it was decided by the
latter that such designation shall be
given only to those lines running between
postoffices. The suggestion of the COM
mittee that letter boxes be placed in
street cars to facilitate the distribution of
mails was favorably received by the
authorities, and suitable boxes are now
being devised for this purpose. The
strike question was vigorously handled
by the convention.

Lock opened the Centenary Exhibition
to-day amid great pomp and display.
Salutes were fred from the
batteries and procession marched
through the streets, headed by

Avenue Of Nations, 1850 yards long, was
lined with troops and seamen from the
Imperial fleet, guarding the grand hall.


The Governor entered the north door
of the hall and was received by the Pres
ident and Executive Committee of the
Exhibition, and =. was conducted to
dais, before which the members
of the Australian Ministry, Supreme Court
and other officers of the Government
were grouped. The Governor then de-
clared the exhibition opened. The Ma
tional hymn was sung by chorus of 800
voices, accom- panied by an orchestra of

WINNIPEG, Man, August 1.-The
terms of the agreement between the
Northern Pacific and the Manitoba Gov
ernment were made public to-day. The
Northern Pacific agrees to build this year
an extension to Portage, and next
year to continue the line to Brandon.
No arrangements have been made
as to branch lines and extensions.
The agreement provides for the main
tentenance of maximum rates from the
Province to Duluth, on wheat and cer-
tain other classes of freight. This rate is
considerably lower than the Canadian
Pacific rate from Winnipeg to Port Ar
thur. The agreement also distinctly
stipulates that the Northern Pacific shall
not enter into any pooling arrangements
with the Canadian Pacific.

Mrs Julia Sophia Walker, OF San Francisco, died
at her home ON Friday night under peculiar cir
cumstances. She was handsome, vigorous
woman, not yet thirty years DID, and mother OF
two children, one a baby and the other about four
years old. Save for their company she was alone
in the evening. She was busy with her household
cares, and the children climbed about her until
shortly after O'Clock, when 1t came their bed
time. She tucked them In their cribs by the fire,
and, kissing them goodnight, turned down the
light that they might sleep the better. Going
then into the parlOr adjoining, she left the door
ajar and, sitting at the piano, played for time in
q soft strain as q lullaby. After time the music
ceased abruptly, and the elder child was aroused
by sound from the parlor like heavy fall. Call
ing its mamma repeatedly and receiving no reply
the little one arose, went into the parlor and
there, by the piano, on the floor just as she had
fallen from the stool, lay the mother, dead. Mr..
Walker reached home within a few minutes there
after and was overwhelmed at the spectacle which
greeted his entrance HIS wife lay dead and his
children were crying with fright. The coroner
was Informed, but, as death plainly resulted from
heart disease, no inquest will be held.

and on being told that it was Nc

feeling of restlessness and insubordina-

the San Carlos reservation for some
months, but open hostilities had been
avoided in every way possible by the
military officials until within few days
past, when several Indians committed
offenses necessitating their arrest. The
attempt to arrest them has caused gen.
eral uprising among them and they
defy the officials and threaten to leave
the reservation. 1t is expected that
they will go south, raiding the settle
ments along the San Pedro river and will
endeavor to reach the Sierra Madre
mountains. Their old rendezvous, the
Santa Catalina mountains, have been
thoroughly secuted by Captain Wint
and Lieutenant Malone within the last
month, from Fort Lowell, to familiarize
themselves with every trail, anticipating
an emergency like this. General alarm
exists among the ranchers and stockmen
on the San Pedro river. Most of the
trouble is anticipated from the Chihuahua
Apaches, Geronimo's tribe.

KNOXVILLE, Tenn, July 1O.-Laurel
Fork meeting house, in Whitmore county,
near Jellico, was the scene last Sunday
of terrible tragedy. 1t was collision
between the Rose and Fusion clans, be-
tween whom feud had existed for some
time. Just as the minister was announc-
ing his text, volley of fire arms was
discharged outside the door. The wor-
shippers were thrown into excitement,
and many women tainted. Outside the
battle ragged fiercely. When the smoke
cleared away it was found that Ewell
Cawson and his son John, belonging to
the Rose faction, were killed, and that
three of the Fusion boys, Tom, Jim and
Enos, and John Porter, belonging to the
other side, were seriously, and perhaps
fatally wounded. A dozen others, whose
names could not be ascertained, were
more or less seriously hurt. Great ex.
citement prevailed, and more trouble is
expected.

Received by the Emperor.


BERLIN, April 24.-Queen Victoria
arrived at Charlottenberg at O'Clock
this morning. The Empress, Grown
Prince and Grown Princess of Sake
Meiningen received her at the depot.
Prince Henry and his sisters, the
Princesses Victoria, Sophia and Mar.
garet, Sir Edward Malet, the British
Ambassador at Berlin, the Duke Of
Rutland, and the Burgomaster and
Municipal Council of Berlin were also
present. The greetings between
Queen Victoria and the royal family
OF Germany were warm The Grown
Prince conducted the Queen to an
open carriage drawn by four horses,
which she entered, and with the EN-
press beside her was driven to the
castle.


Crowds of people lined the route
and cheered enthusiastically as the
carriage passed. The Queen paid
visit to the Emperor shortly after her
arrival at the castle. The doctors
feared that the meeting would excite
the Emperor and probably upset him,
but their fears were groundless. The
Emperor seemed rather bright after
the interview and his temperature
was more normal.


NEWSPAPER COMMENT.


The North German Gazette, referring
to the visit of the Queen of England,
says: "Her Majesty will be welcomed
by the whole population of Germany,
and, above all, by the inhabitants Of
Berl n, with the veneration and SYM
pathy so Justly due to one who has for
SO many years ruled friendly state,
and who is the mother of our Empress.
All German hearts will thankfully &C
cept, as token of the Queens deep
sympathy for the fate Of our reigning
house, the fact that she comes to the
sick bed of our beloved Emperor and
personally shares the deep affliction
and deep anxiety with which we are
filed to-day. May she be enabled to
bring comfort and hope, and when
she departs from Germany to take
with her the assurance that the SYM
pathy she has displayed will always
be kept in grateful remembrance
here!"


HOW SHE SPENT THE DAY.


BERLIN, April 24.-Queen Victoria
and the Empress drove out with the
Prince and Princess Of Sake Meinin-
gen. The streets were crowded and
the Queen and Empress were greeted
with enthusiasm. The Queen made
three visits to the sick room of the
Emperor, who is keeping his bed until
he gets stronger. He has been
in excellent spirits and had
several refreshing maps. The
meeting between Queen Victoria
and her daughter, the Empress, this
morning, was very touching. They
embraced and kissed each other re-
peatedly. The Queen went immedi-
ately to see the Emperor and was
astonished and delighted to find him
looking better than she expected.
She will depart tomorrow unless the
Emperor should have a relapse,

Byrnes' men, who found him at Stamford,

ally resisting three burglars, led by Dinarvo,

stronghold. They secured over 100, 900 francs.

Italy. Two of the robbers were caught in the
mountains. They confessed and betrayed

ST. PAUL, September 1.-THE Pioneer
Press account of the frightful accident
this morning at Wicks tunnel on the
Montana Central road, twenty miles from
Helena, says: About 6 o'clock this morn
ing the night shift were engaged in put
ting in their last charge. There were
about thirty or forty men at the south
heading and twenty-five in the north.
Charges of giant powder had
been put in the north headings,
and it was calculated to set
them both off at once. The men in
the south end were just leaving the head
ing to get in safe place when fearful
explosion shook the mountain, over
whelmed the wcrkmen, blew some of
them to atoms and buried others under
rocks and earth. Those who were in the
lead on the way out escaped unhurt, but
the rear of the crowd caught the full
force of the explosion. Several were
killed outright and number of others
severely wounded. The survivors escaped
to the outer air and gave the alarm,
when the work of rescue was begun. The
bodies were removed and laid out along
the track at the mouth of the tunnel,
where they presented a ghastly spectacle.
Six wounded men were also taken from
the debris, only one OF whom is seriously
hurt. They were brought into Helena
this afternoon for medical treatment.
The names of the killed are !:
James Mullens, Hans Peterson, Mike


Welsh, David Walker, Thos. Pierson,


VIM. Vale, Frank Anderson, John Sand
berg, Geo. Irving and one unknown. Ir-
ving's head was completely severed from
the body. The others were horribly mu-
tilated. The cause was the exploding of
signal cap in the north heading, which
touched off the powder in long hole
charged from the south heading. The


dead bodies were brought to Helena for
interment.

Early large crowds began to congre-

drew knife and stabbed the officer in the

at Conway. The ball struck the other officer,
Deputy Sheriff Lloyd, in the breast, inficting
. fatal wound. Witt fell exhausted from the
loss of blood, and late adyices say neither of
the officers will recover.

way, but those who know him say he will not
be taken alive. The affair has created great
excitement.

STOCKTON, August 4.-John Chamber
lain, laboring man about 80 years old,
shot his wife, probably fatally, and killed
himself shortly before O'Clock this
afternoon. The neighbors were startled
by hearing three shots and almost i'm
mediately the woman ran out with bloo'
running over her clothing. She was car
Iied into friends house and the ply
sic;ans afterward removed her to the
county hospital. The neighbors fearing
to 60 in the house where the murderer
was, telephoned for officers, and Sheriff
Cunningham soon arrived and with
others entered the shanty, finding the
body of Chamberlain with bullet hole
in the center of the forehead. He lived
nearly an hour but did not speak. The
physicians postponed probing the
woman's wound until tomorrow. She
was shot in the right ear, but the ball
Can be felt short distance back. It is
feared the skull has been fractured and
death may follow, but tonight she was
resting quietly.


The woman says her husband asked
her to get him something from a room,
and as she came out he shot her. She
fell and rolled out the front door just as
he shot again. She regained her feet
and ran, when the third shot,
which killed him, was fred.
She told the Coroner that her husband
abused her great deal, and was very
jealous, but without cause. At times he
acted strangely, and month ago got up
in the night and took pistol to kill her,
but was persuaded to put it away. He
had done but little work for the past two
months, and frequent quarrels were
heard by the neighbors. Last week he
went away, looking for work, and on re-
turning charged his wife with having
been away from home at night during
his absence. She had kept house some
years ago for an old man named Hunt
ington, living near this city, and Cham
berlin frequently charged her with car
ing too much for the old man. An in
quest was held and a verdict found in
accordance with the facts.

NEW YORK, July 1S.-The North Ger
man Lloyd steamship Fulda which ar
rived yesterday from Bremen run down
an unknown fishing schooner on

A dense fog prevailed at that time and
the shoOner disappeared astern immed-

search of her and for nearly an hour
groped around in the fog but no traces of
the schooner nor twenty of the men be-

sengerss son the steamer were Mortified
witnesses to the collision. The lost ves-
sci was probably French fisherman.

ual precautions were being. taken when
the collision occurred.

Gustave Schwab, agent OF the North
German Lloyd line in this city, said to-
day that the public reports of the collis-
ion were grossly exaggerated. Capt.
Ringk's official report, Agent Schwab
said, stated that the Fulda struck the
schooner in a dense fog, carrying away

not touched. The passengers on deck of
the steamer at the time grew excited and
threw number of life preservers over
board, but this precaution was unneces-
sary. The cause of the accident accord
ing to the captains statement was the
neglect of the fisherman to sound its
bells during the fog.

wreck was the fact that freight, which
was moving slowly, struck the obstruc-

engineer of the freight train to slow up

early hour all the express passengers

SAN Francisco, September 6.-Tht


story of the wreck OF the Arctic whaling


fleet is substantially as follows:


During the latter part of July the Arc


tic fleet kept we'll together, while work
ing to the north and east of Behrins
Straits. Much ice was encountered, the


season was late, but few whales were


seen, and finally the vessels reached


Point Barrow, having caught compare
lively nothing. The long Arctic day was
spent in spent in searching for an open
ing to the north, but without avail, and


the evening of August I'd found about
thirty steamers and barks riding at an
chor somewhat southerly of Point Bar
row. Towards evening a brisk breeze
set in from the southwest, and with it
the sea grew heavier and heavier, and
by 6 O'Clock the following morning
the masters of the vessels were con.
vinced that it would be sheer
folly to seek shelter from the storm
where they were, and the wind blowing
towards Point Barrow; all anchors were
weighed and the vessels turned the Point
where they were seemingly sheltered
from the storm. All day OF the Sd the
gale blew with undiminished violence,
whipping the sea into foaming, seeth-
ing mass. Suddenly towards night, the
wind again changed, exposing the whal-
ers to the utm ost fury of the sea. The
vessels were anchored comparatively near
the shore. The steamers at once put
into deeper water but with the sailing
vessels some Of the anchors would not
come loose. Some were lost altogether,
ond with only few minutes warning the
unfortunate ships were tossing about in
the breakers occasionally striking with
tremendous force on the bottom.


The Young Ph@nix's crew couldn't
weigh anchor rapidly enough, and she
struck again and again, till with the hull
all smashed she drifted to the eastward
at the mercy of the storm. The Mary
and Susan didn't get loose at all, but
thumped the bottom till the storm was
over. She was total wreck. The
Fleetwing finally got free and was cast
ward a few miles, totally wrecked. and
her crew were saved by the steam
whalers.


The Jane Gray became unmanageable,
AVID was cast against huge cake of ice,
and though finally headed for the An
drew Hicks, sank before she reached
that vessel Her crew were picked up.


A long list of minor disa ters are re-
corded and the whaling men can remem-
Der no such disastrous season for years,
except that of about a year ago, when
the whole feet was last.


The catch at the latest accounts had
been only twenty-five whales, when last
year over three hundred were taken.
The steamer Orca alone caught more
than the fleet has done this year.


The young Phoenix had taken one
whale which had been transferred to
the tender before the disaster.

The glorious Gospel of Peace and Love has
not vet eliminated all strife and self-seeklng
from human society. The necessary conse-
ouence is that there are still suffering and
want ignorance, brutality and crime. Against
these the preachers and the officers Of law, the
teachers the moralists and the reformers, strug-
gle not always with encouraging success. At
times hope grows dim, and the CHASTITY spec
tacle of human suffering kindles in honest
hearts a flame OF indignation. Benevolence
bends over the manned and broken with
zeal not always wise in its remedies. The
spirit of reform sometimes grows passionate IN
the presence of obstacles which seem lmpreg-
nable and eternal. And yet does the world
MAKE no progress from one Christmas Day to
another? is there not, in spite of all, sure
and steady gain for all that is best and highest
in human endeavorP


The wear does not always include both seed
time and harvest in moral and social helds,
and the worrhiest achievements of 1888 may
not be realized until eyes now bright with
youth and purpose shall be dimmed with age
But looking back little distance along the
pathway trodden by any nation, can we not
comprehend that the change for the better has
been far beyond the widest hopes of the most
sanguine? Not many generations have passed
since the English laborer was in all essentials
slave, and the victim of expressions which
would now appear intolerable. France knew
only a people mad with suffering, and aristo-
Gratis mad with terror. Russia had sefdom,
Brazil slavery, within the lifetime Of men not
yet old, and even this free Republic sent back
fugitive slaves At what other period in the
worlds history has labor been so well reward
ed or so comfortable in condition and clrcum-
stances as it is now? Always, as now, the
workers have been the great majority, and
their condition has determined the condition
of the people as a whole. 1t is not necessary
to dig down, with Professor Thorold Rogers
into long buried records of early English life |;
at his best and highest, the worker OF that day
| lived in his serfdom life which no laborer OF
to-day however needy, would consent to live.
The centuries have brought great changes, and
the movement has not been always in one dl-
rection, but the great and lasting changes have
all been for the uplifting, the freedom and the
happiness Of mankind. Even in this land
where patriotic ancestors planted religious ana
civil freedom with the rareS. opportunities, each
half century has brought new world ana new
life. During the recent campaign millions
learned from public discussion something OF
the changes wrought since 1860. One party
holds that those wonderful and beneficent
changes have largely resulted from its policy
the other, that they have come in spite of that
policy but no party disputes that they have
! in effect created a new and happier world for
American workers. Better houses better
food. more suitable and abundant clothing,
education inaccessible and comforts never mag
ined thirty years ago are now within the reach
of every honest worker, through better re-
turns for less eXhauSting toll.


If there is much to be accomplished, all past
experience gives ground for hope. The better
and brighter age advances in which the
brotherhood of mankind shall be everywhere
recognized, not only in word but in deed, not
only at voting-places but in workshops and in
all relations of life. 1t advances in spite OF all
hindrances, conQuering crime subdung pas
sion. making education and uplifting for all
necessary to the interest Of each, and compel
ling even human selfShness to labor for its
/ fastening.

west of Martins Ferry. The tunnel is 500 feet In
length, one-hah Of which is completed WORK was
begun on 1t last August, since which time over 100
men have been working I'm It, The contractors are
Miller & McMann, OF New-York. At the opening
of the tunnel stood the blacksmith shop Fifty feet

this Is the dynamite Along short Creek, ABOUT
100 yards west Of this opening stood four buildings
One of these, measuring sixteen by forty feet and
stories high, occupied by the coiored laoor
ers. Adjoining this another building, the same
size which occupied by the italian iaborers, and
little further south a still larger building
known as the boardln house, in which the better

tity OF powder and dynamite, blown to atoms

ing house and the commissary we're partially wrecked
One thousand yards from the general boarding house

COLUMBUS, O., September 4.-The Ohio
Centennial Exposition opened this morn.
ing. The city was profusely decorated.
The streets were crowded with visitors to
the great agricultural, mechanical and
stock show at the fair grounds. Six
thousand Ohio militia paraded this
morning and were received by Governor
Foraker. The Governor will start the
machinery this afternoon.


The immense amphitheatre in which
the exercises were held was crowded
when Governor Foraker began the ex-
ercises by requesting the singing of the
"Doxology," the large audience being
led by welltrained choir of l, ,450 chill
dren. The first chorus was Centennial
song. which gave an account of the pros
perity of the State and Nation. Director
General Hurst then presented the work
of the Centennial Commission to Gov
ernor Foraker, who in strong speech
presented it to the public. Hon. Coates
Kinney, the author of the well-known
poem, "Rain on the Roof" read the Cen
tennial ode, which considered the past
hundred years in labor, knowledge, free
dom and peace, and was full of good
points. Mrs. Governor Foraker touched
the electric button and started the
machinery, and the Ohio centennial was
under way.

Associated Press Dispatches to the HERALD
TRUCKEE, CAL, December 25.-The


express car on the east-bound overland


train was robbed last night two miles
east of Clipper Gap. Bod Johnson, the
express messenger, says he was sitting
at his desk and his helper was sorting


out packa ges to be left at Colfax, when
suddenly the glass transoms over the
two doors, one on each side of the car,


were broken in simultaneously, and two
revolvers thrust through, covering


both messengers. Johnson was
compelled to :open the door ard
let one robber in, being ordered to keep
one hand held up. The other robber
reached inside and unlatched the door,
letting himself in. He then covered the
messenger while the first robber took
from the safe all the coin packages,
which he placed in game pouch slung
across his shoulder. Between Clipper
Gap and Applegate, the grade is heavy
and takes fifteen minutes to run two and
a half miles. The robbers had no difficulty
therefore in jumping from the train,
and the entire transaction occupied less
than five minutes. When the train
stopped at New England Mills, tramp
who was on the front end Of the baggage
car ran toward and told the engineer that
the express car had been robbed. The
conductors were notified and the party
knocked at the door of the express Car.
The messengers, who thought the robbers
were still on the train, would not open
the doors sfor some minutes. One
messenger says he pulled the bell cord
but the engineers deny this. The
messengers gave a description of the rob-
bers, who were only partially disguised,
and were both young men. They were
apparently well acquainted with the
route and with the habits of the messen-
gers. The descriptions were telegraphed
in different directions from Colfax, and
two tramps were held as witnesses. The
loss may reach into the thousands.

every day the record would be broken.

tory, and the party set out at something
less than 2:20 rate for the station,

on charge of fast driving. They will
visit Justice Kings room this morning.

Last Sunday week, says the Natal
South Africa Witness, one of the most
remarkable scenes on record is reported
as having been witnessed in the vicinity
of Table Mountain. A troop of cattle,
consisting of twelve COWS and patri-
archal old bull, were grazing on one of
the plateau-like spurs of the mountain,
which is surrounded on three sides by
precipitous ravines and on the fourth
side, that nearest the mountain, by
dense bush. Some natives higher up
the mountain were attracted by the
sudden believing of the cattle, and
saw two enormous pythons coming
out of the bush and making for
the cattle. which had drawn them
selves up in compact group, the bull
at it's head. AS the pythons drew near
the animals gradually backed till they
stood on small space that jutted out
over tremendous precipice. At this
stage sudden rush was made. but only
one heifer succeeded in escaping. The
other cattle lowing in the most piteous
manner, gradually backed and one by
one fell over the precipice. till finally
only the bull was left. He suddenly
charged at the biggest python, transfix-
ing the reptile on his horns, but the
second snake seized the bull in its folds
and, having it's tail around a
huge bowlder, commenced to crush
the bull, which, moaning piteously
struggled frantically to escape. The tail
of the python lost its hold of the rock
but the larger snake, which had slipped
off the horn, tapping its tail around a
smaller bowlder opposite the one the
other snake had just released, selzed the
bull and compressed the animal in its
scaly folds. The other python succeeded
in regaining its former position and the
bull was literally suspended in mid-air
by the snakes. The whole scene looked
like some ghastly triumphal arch. The
snakes were evidently getting the
best of the poor brute, which was bleed
ing profusely, when, by sudden effort,
his struggles forced both reptiles to
loose their held of the rocks. and the
whole three were hurled into the ravine
beneath. The cattle were found ON the
first ledge of the precipice, all being
dead, but the bull and the pythons had
bounded from ledge to ledge, and were
fonnd 400 feet below the scene of the
fight. The bull was merely mangled
mass, and the snakes were greatly mutt.
lated, the larger one having the vertebre
broken in nine places. The pythons,


which were of the rock species, were
male and female, and measured respec.
lively 40 feet 8 inches, and SO feet 81
| inches.

Terrible State of Destitution In


Ramsey County, Dakota


MINNEAPOLIS, October 23.-J. Harp
man, who has just returned from another
visit to Ramsey county, Dakota, says of
the Polish Jew sufferers there, that the
settlement is seventeen miles from
DEVILS Lake and comprises seventy fami-
lies, numbering 23S souls. They came
here two years ago laet spring, procured
land, built houses and went to work
to clear land and become independent
farmers. Those without money mort
gagged their land and borrowed enough
to pay the Government price. They
raised fair crop the first year and their
prospects were 80 bright that they mort
gagged their lands and other property to
purchase stock and farm machines.
The second year they planted q
much larger acreage. The notes and
mortgages signed By them bore ex.
horbitant interest About the middle of
August severe frost came and ruined
the entire wheat crop, leaving them only
about as many potatoes as they used for
planting, and barely enough oats to win
ter their stock. Trouble and suffering
began at once. Merchants who hereto
fore had been anxious to supply all their
wants refused to credit them any more.
Nearly every creditor became alarmed
and foreclosed. The situation became go
bad that the Sheriff refused to inflict
further suffering on the psople by taking
their property. He found them without
fuel or bread; they were usingthe drop
pings Of cattle for fuel to cook snch arti.
cles as they could get. Men, women and
children were in rags and without food.


"We found everything as the sheriff
had stated" said Mr.. Harpman. "For
the present their most pressing needs
are fuel and bread. and these articles
must be had at once, for every day is
suffering and priviation. We visited
about twenty houses and found. all,
with but two exceptions, without stick
of wood or any other material for
fire except cattle droppings. On Satur-
day the ice was three-fourths of an inch
thick and we found numerous little
children with bare feet and legs. One
woman with two little girls, with bare
feet and limbs, was trying to keep warm
on the sunny side of the house. Some
creditor had taken her COW and left her
to starve with her little ones.

The Atlas Sunk.


New York, October 23.-The steamer
Atlas, OF the Atlas line, bound from Port
Lemon, having left that port on the 18th
instant, was sunk this evening off Vesey
street. The steamer was struck on the
starboard bow by the ferryboat Central,
and ten minutes later the Atlas sunk.
The ferry-boat struck the steamer on the
bow. The only thing to be seen OF the
sunken vessel are her topmasts and fun
nels. The Atlas was coming up the
river at a low speed There was fog at
the time. The steamer was about 500
yards out from the docks. The
bow of the Central crashed into
the Atlas and bent the iron plates
like so many pieces of board. For
a second or two the Atlas trembled and
listed, and then began to sink, bow first,
so that soon the propeller was out of the
water. When the collision occurred all
hands on board the Atlas were ordered
on deck. The engineer obeyed the
summons without stopping the engine,
so that the propeller whirled round and
round in the air. In this position the
steamer remained for about five min.
utes. The vessel then plunged forward
and went down, apparently settling on
an easy keel. AS the steamer began to
sink the crew and all hands took to the
rigging. Just at this juncture tug boat
steamed alongside and took off all on
board.

quet Theater last night, an explosion
of gas occurred and the theater took
fire and was destroyed. The house
was full Of spectators, and number
of lives were lost. Ten bodies have
been recovered from the ruins, and
many persons were injured.

Eight bodies have been taken from
the ruins. Most of those burned were
in the third row of the boxes and gal
leries, where whole families were euf-
focated. There was terrific struggle
at the door when the spectators tried
to escape. Large numbers were suf-
focated and trampled upon. Nearly
all of the victims were spectators.

tunes. Many in the theatre finding
themselves unable to reach the doors
jumped from the windows. Several
corpses were found in the stage boxes.

triple tragedy was enacted in the
country near here last evening.
Henry Miller and William Oderholt
farmers, had lawsuit over trivial
matter and Miller, the loser, swore he
would get even. After the trial Mil
Ter, true to his word, shouldered his
rifle and went to field where L. G.
Kinsey, one of Oderholt's witnesses,
was blowing. Miller first killed
Kinsey's horse and then shot Kin
sey twice, inflicting mortal wounds.
Then he went to another field
where Oderholt was at work. Oder
holt's horse was first slain by Miller,
and then Oderholt himself. 1t is
supposed that Kinsey and Oderholt
attempted to shield themselves be-
hind their horses. When his revenge
was completed, Miller proceeded to
the hut which served as his home,
and after setting the place on fire,
blew his own brains out. His black
ened corpse was found in the debris.

knife. Miller was a foreigner. forty
years old, and lived alone. Kinsey
and Oderholt were among the most
respected citizens of the county.

RECEDING OF THE TIDE.


ST. PAUL, MISN.. Dec. PA Port Town
send. w. T.. special to the PIONEER Press SAYS:
The steamship Idaho arrived from Alaskan
ports last evening bringing news concerning
the wreck of the steam schooner Leo at Prince
Frederick sound. about 20 miles southeast of
Juneau. on November %. The Leo left Seattle
one month previous laden with general cargo
Of furs. When stormy weather ensued she went
into Prince Frederick sound and anchored
The tide receded and the storm abated and the
Leo was left high and dry on a ledge of Table
Rock. The vessel settled down a distance of
10 feet striking her stern on rocky boulders
and completely demolishing the keel The
tide fell "a feet. The crew landed ON the
beach, half mile distant. and saved nearly all
the vessels gear. The whole cargo was lost
boat with five men was sent to Juneau for
assistance, and the rest of the crew remained
on the beach for twenty-five days waiting for
assistance. Capt. Whitford and the cook re-
manned at the scene of the disaster guarding
the saved material. The Leo sustained iniu-
ries which are irreparable and the vessel is a
total wreck. The steam schooner Leo was built
at Baltimore, Md, as a United States revenue
cutter. She was constructed of Florida liveoak
and was considered one of the staunchest cut
tiers in the service. After her arrival ON this
coast she cruised on Puget sound and Alaska.
at one time being fifteen months in Sitka har-
Dor, at another eleven months. She was finally
condemned and bought by San Francisco par
ties. Under their ownership she made frequent
trips to the Arctic, the most notable being the
transfer Of Lieut.. Ray and his party of the
United States coast survey to Point Barron. and
her subsequent return two years later TO San
Francisco. She also carried the famous miner
and frontiersman, Scheffelin, to the Yukon
river with his stern-wheel steamer New Racket
Capt. A. T.Whitford, of the Sitka Trading COM
pany, recently refused Sl2, 900 for the Leo. The
cargo was very valuable.

returned on Burke's chin. After sparring

Oregon has woman mail-carrier. Her
name is Miss Minnie Westman, and she
corries Uncle Sans mail from the head
of navigation on Siuslaw River over the
Coast range mountains, following up the
river to Hale's Postoffice station, within
fifteen miles of Eugene City.


Her route is twenty miles long and is
situated right in the heart of the noun
tains, where all the dangers and adven-
lures incident to such an occupation
abound. She carries the mail night and
day and fears nothing. She rides horse
back and carries revolver.


Miss Westman is plump little brun-
cite, and is just twenty years old. Her
father and uacle operate a stage line,
and have a contract for carrying the
mail. At Hale's station Minnie meets
her father and gets the mail from Eugene
City and starts on her round.


Miss Westman has never met with a
serious mishap in the performance of her
duty. On one OF her trips last year she
found three good-sized bears in the road
right in front of her. The horse, on es-
pying them, became frightened, threw
his rider to the ground and turning
around, ran back the road he came.
Miss Westman, with great presence
OF mind, started after the runaway
and, overtaking him, remounted
and rode right through the
savage Gordon, and, strange to say, she
was not attacked. Meeting some friends,
she told them Of what she had seen, and
they went to the place and killed the
bears. So far this year Miss Westman
has met two bears, which did not modest
her. Portland Oregonian.

VALLEJO, February 27.-This morn
ing there happened the most terrible
fatality in the history of Vallejo.
About ten minutes after six, just af-
ter the whistle had blown to signal
ize the departure of the steamer
Julia from the South Vallejo wharf on
her first trip and before she had got
loose from her moorings, a terrific
explosion occurred, rocking the YES
sci through its whole extent, and fill
ing the air with smoke. The early
trip takes all the workmen living on
the Vallejo side to work in various in
dustries on the Contra Costa side
also those going to San Francisco.
Consequently great many passen-
gers were ON board. The morning
being cool, most of them had gath
cred around the warm smoke stack in
the lower cabin. As the explosion
came from the boiler, these men
were directly exposed to the terrible
shock. Besides this the petroleum
used for fuel was scattered through
the steamer, setting it on fire. There
was terrible confusion and heart
rending cries from the crushed
and burning men.


THE FORCE OF THE EXPLOSION
Is shown on body that was dragged
out Of the wreck by Constable Longan
without head or limbs, utterly unrec.
ognizable. The burning steamer set
fire to the wharf, and for hours the
flames held sway until the boat was
burned to the waters edge. AS far as
can be learned, eight or ten are killed
or missing and many badly injured.


1t is declared that there were sixty.
seven people on board, of whom only
seventeen have been accounted for
and the fear is now entertained thai
the calamity is much more serious
than at first thought, indicating that
fortysspersons at the outside were
killed.


THE DISASTER WAS DUE


To the explosion of one of the petro
leum vats, and within few minutes
after the explosion the steamer sanl
in the mud. The water now covers
her upper deck, and all that can bt
seen Of her is the flagstaff. The
wharf caught fire and is still burning
The telegraph Office was also de
stroyed. The full scope OF the dis
aster cannot be known for severa
days.


When the news of the disaster
reached North Vallejo the fire depart
ment turned out, but was unable to dc
anything towards saving the wharf
The Starr Touring mills were
threatened, but luckily escaped.
There was no water to combat the
fire, and as the tide was out the
engines were unable to go to work.
Over 600 feet OF wharf was destroye 4,
but the fire was under control by
o'clock.


THE CASUALTY LIST.


Five bodies have been recovered so
far. They are Michael Brannelly
Albert Madison, Oliff Nelson and
two burned beyond recognition
John Oliver was rescued alive, but
died from his injuries. 1t is believed
that ten bodies still remain on the
steamer. Captain Gedge and most oi
the crew escaped with slight injuries


Among the missing are Edward and
James Rule, John Campton, Timothy
Hurley, Joseph Williams, William
Connolloy, John Hodgkins, Michael
Dolan, William Lamar, John CLARK
and Z. G. Mcdonald.


UP TO ONE O'CLOCK


Nine bodies had been recovered, but
only seven were identified: Joseph
Fragas, longshoreman; William
Loman, shipping clerk; Melvin
Hodgkins, tallyman for Puget Sound
Lumber Co. and a man named Hig.
gins.


THE CORONER AT WORK.
At 4 O'Clock it was known that out
Of the missing men there remained
still ten to account for. Deputy Cor
oner Whitaker, who had been on the
scene all day, decided to hold an in
quest, for the purpose of identifying
the bodies. From the many stand
ing around he speedily selected a
jury, and after they had been sworn,
Identification commenced. The work
was not easy, as all of the bodies
were more or less disfgured. In one
corner of the shed lay mass of hui
man remains, charred, bruised
and mangled beyond recogni-
tion. Near by lay a second, the
skull frightfully disfgured, and
one hand blowa off. A third was the
body of a young man, the face raw
with burns, legs broken, and pre-
senting pitiful spectacle. Many
men were married, and leave families.
In the shed only jurors and press
representatives were allowed, but
outside there were crowds of anxious
ones, and many cry was heard, as,
peering over the gates or between the
bars, glimpse was caught of some
familiar body. When the jury's
labors were suspended they had iden-
titled thirteen, and by inquiry among
those around.

A very interesting fight for blood took
place yesterday evening about O'Clock
near where the Santa Fe track crosses
Roy street. Two ,bus-drivers who are
known by the names Of Doughnuts and
Boston Beans had been aching for some
time to settle the question of supremacy
and pursuant to agreement met at the
above named place where a ring was
staked off and fight with bare knuckles
commenced. The first round was
devoted by both ,Doughnuts and Beans
endeavoring to find the others weak
joints, and it did not begin to become in
teresting until toward the close. Beans
was just preparing to land right handler
somewhere on Doughnuts physiognomy
when time was called.


The second round was much livelier.
Doughnuts forced the fighting and drew
first blood. Heavy blows were ex-
changed, and Beans retired to his corner
in rather ratified condition.


Doughnuts got the worst of the fight in
the third round. Beans managed to land
a left handler on Doughnuts eye, and the
rest of the round was uninteresting.


Doughnuts, however, came up smiling
for the fourth round, and displayed such
activity that Beans was thought to have
lost the fight.


The fifth round was hot one. Beans
got his blood up and went at it hammer
and tongs. the result being that Dough
nuts threw up the sponge.


A sorrier sight than the two bus
drivers has seldom been seen. Both
wore marks that time alone can efface
A steak was applied to Doughnut's eye
but it disappeared. There were ten wit.
nesses to the fight. Young Riley was
time-keeper and Dutch Jake was referee

company wanted a test case made
